title: Graph traversal with BFS and DFS
explanation:
Store a graph as an **adjacency list**: a dict mapping each vertex to the list of its neighbours. Both standard traversals start at a source vertex, visit everything reachable from it, and **never visit a vertex twice** — keep a `seen` set and mark a vertex when you first *discover* it, so it can't be queued or pushed again. With that rule, both run in O(V + E) time: every vertex is processed once and every edge looked at once (O(V) extra space for `seen` and the frontier).

**Breadth-first search (BFS)** explores in rings: first the source, then all vertices one edge away, then two edges away, and so on. That is why, in an *unweighted* graph, BFS finds **shortest paths** (fewest edges). Its frontier is a FIFO queue (`collections.deque`): vertices are expanded in the order they were discovered, nearest first.

**Depth-first search (DFS)** follows one path as far as it can, then backs up to the most recent vertex with an unexplored edge. Its frontier is a stack (or the call stack, if you write it recursively). DFS answers *reachability* questions — "can I get there?", "how many connected pieces?" — but the path it finds is **not** necessarily the shortest.

To cover a graph that isn't connected, loop over all vertices and start a new traversal from each one that hasn't been seen yet; each start discovers one connected component.
keyIdeas: Adjacency list + `seen` set; mark vertices when first discovered.
BFS (queue) explores by distance and finds fewest-edge paths.
DFS (stack/recursion) goes deep, then backtracks; good for reachability.
Both are O(V + E) time with adjacency lists.

workedExample.problem: Rooms are numbered 0…n-1; `keys[r]` lists the rooms whose keys lie in room r. You start in room 0. Can you open every room? Use `keys = [[1, 3], [3, 0, 1], [2], [0]]`.
steps: Model it as a directed graph: an edge r → k for every key k found in room r.
The question is reachability from room 0, so any traversal works — use iterative DFS with a stack.
Mark a room as seen when its key is first found, before pushing it, so no room is pushed twice.
Trace: open 0 → keys 1, 3; open 3 → key 0 (seen); open 1 → keys 3, 0, 1 (all seen). Room 2's key is only inside room 2, so it is never reached.
workedExample.answer: `False` — rooms 0, 1, and 3 are reachable, but room 2 is not. Each room and each key is handled once, so the check is linear in rooms + keys.

pitfalls: Marking vertices as visited when they are *popped* instead of when discovered, so the same vertex is queued many times.
Using DFS when the question asks for the fewest steps — only BFS guarantees that in an unweighted graph.
Forgetting vertices with no edges (or unreachable parts) when counting components.

Solves Single Source Reachability, not SSSP.
